$comment: The repository settings that are NOT code — branch rules and merge policy — written down because nothing else can hold them. A clone carries every gate in this tree, and none of these: delete the repository and they are gone, recreate it and they come back as GitHub's defaults, which are not these. This is a record, not an enforcer: no gate compares it to reality, because doing so needs an admin token this repository's sessions do not hold. Apply it with `gh api --method POST repos/ecoma-io/runtime-trail/rulesets --input <a ruleset entry>` once `main` exists (ruleset conditions name `~DEFAULT_BRANCH`, which does not resolve until the first push), and read live state back with `GET /repos/ecoma-io/runtime-trail/rulesets` to diff it against this file. The full tier-by-tier arithmetic this shape was derived from — Scorecard's `Branch-Protection` check, what each rule buys and what each deliberately forfeits — lives in `ecoma`'s `.github/repository-settings.json` and is not restated here; this file records the decisions and points there for the derivations.

repository.$comment: Merge policy. Exactly one method stays enabled, so the strategy is a mechanism rather than whichever button someone clicked. Merge commits, matching every product repository in this organisation: a branch's commits land on main as the SAME objects, which is what makes `delete_branch_on_merge` safe (it removes a pointer, not history) and `git revert -m 1` the one undo that works.

rules.$comment: The default branch cannot be deleted outright, and cannot be force-pushed, which would rewrite landed history and silently invalidate every commit pinned off it — the merge queue's would-be-trunk runs included. These two are Scorecard `Branch-Protection` Tier 1; that check awards nothing above them until BOTH are present.

required_approving_review_count is 0 — see `notAppliedYet.reviewApprovalNeedsASecondHuman` in ecoma's copy of this file: GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, this repository has one maintainer, and the required checks plus the merge queue are the actual gate. `require_code_owner_review: true` covers the three legal files `.github/CODEOWNERS` names. `allowed_merge_methods` must stay `['merge']` and must agree with the merge_queue rule below — a queue configured to squash would quietly undo this decision.

`integration_id` 15368 is GitHub Actions: it pins the check to the app that produces it, so a differently-owned check of the same name cannot satisfy it. Both gates are single aggregating jobs on purpose — one name each, so adding a CI or analysis job never means remembering to edit repository settings (a job left out of `needs` in its gate is simply ungated, which the gate's own file documents). `strict_required_status_checks_policy: true` makes the queue re-run these on the would-be trunk rather than trusting the branch run.

The merge queue, matching the organisation's policy: an approved pull request does not merge directly, it queues and the gates re-run on the would-be trunk — main plus the entries ahead of it. `ALLGREEN` is what makes that real rather than decorative: a batch lands only if every entry in it passes together, so two individually-green changes that are wrong combined fail the batch instead of landing. THIS RULE HAS A CODE DEPENDENCY: the queue waits for `ci-gate` and `analysis-gate` to report on the temporary queue ref, so both workflows must list `merge_group` among their triggers — they do. Removing that trigger and keeping this rule is the failure mode (a queue that accepts pull requests and merges none, silently); they change together or not at all.

notAppliedYet.$comment: One entry, about the distance between this file and the live repository. Everything above is target state: the repository was created empty and had no rulesets when this file was written (verified over the public API — `GET /repos/ecoma-io/runtime-trail/rulesets` returned `[]`), and applying them needs an admin token. Until they are applied, main is protected by nothing but the hooks every commit already carries. After the first push, apply the ruleset, then diff live state against this file — a stale entry here is worse than none, because it reads as a known gap when it is really an unread one.
notAppliedYet.branchRules: Target state only, nothing applied yet. Apply order: push `main` first (the ruleset's condition needs a default branch), then `POST /repos/ecoma-io/runtime-trail/rulesets` with the entry above. The published OpenSSF Scorecard `Branch-Protection` score will read this ruleset over the public GraphQL API once applied — rulesets are readable without an admin token where classic branch protection is not — so the published score is a live audit of the rules above.
